Introduction - June 2010 











##### **Introduction** 

There have been further LME metal price declines as sentiment remains negative towards the industrial commodities.  The GFMS base metal index on 3rd June at 249.5 was 23% down from the high for the year.  However given the extraordinary gains seen in 2009 and early 2010, our index is still up 20% year-on-year. 

In our recent analysis of the steel market, we questioned whether prices were merely dipping from an earlier overbought position or were entering a more severe downturn. We

came to the conclusion that it was a dip. For base metals, where investment flows play a much more important role, the answer to the question is less clear cut. The other concern about pricing is the less price elastic response of the base metals industry; we are already seeing production cutbacks in the steel market. A lot of attention has been focused on the impact of Greece and the threat of contagion to other Mediterranean economies and then, more seriously, the potential for the more robust northern European economies to be dragged into the mire. In early June, these themes continue to be the single most important driver of price movements for the base metals complex. As we are going to publication, loss of confidence regarding the United States - until recently alleged to be on the path of recovery - was added to the woes of Europe, as worse than expected US jobs data emerged on 4th June. These factors have obviously “spooked” the markets, culminating in notably lower base metal prices. However there is some good news relating to the sector in that our discussions with leading semi-fabricators and steel mills still point to the recovery in demand being sustained. In addition, most of the economic indicators that we track remain in positive territory. ###### **~~Base Metals & Other Commodity Prices~~** 250

Of perhaps great concern to the base metals sector in the short term (certainly over the summer months) are developments in China. This is reflected in a slowdown in the rate of growth in some of the key economic aggregates. Equally importantly, production within the country, at both the concentrate and refined metal stage is rising sharply. Another feature, which is more difficult to quantify, is that an element of destocking may be underway for some metals. The Chinese trade data for base metals is still probably the best and most comprehensive way of assessing the wider changes in the market balance within China. For aluminium and lead, China has turned from being a net importer to a net exporter. For nickel, tin and zinc, net imports have fallen away, but, somewhat surprisingly, net imports of copper cathode have held up reasonably well so far this year (up to April). However, GFMS believe that the data for the next few months will tell a different story. More encouraging for the base metals sector is that figures relating to non-ferrous semis production are still strong. At this stage, we still believe that any demand weakness from China will be a temporary phenomenon. This view is reflected in our supply-demand balance and price projections. In this issue of the Base Metals One Year Forecast, we have extended the quarterly projections out to the second quarter

of next year. In terms of prices, the bulk of the change reflects the lower base that we are seeing in June compared to early year peaks. We have amended our balances to take into account greater uncertainty on the demand side, and we note that prices have not fallen far enough to bring about a supply response (see individual sections for our revised supply-demand and price forecasts). ###### **~~Base Metals Prices in Major Currencies~~** 250

The Conference Board index of consumer confidence jumped again in May to 63.3 from 57.7. Encouragingly the expectations component again led the gain, up to 85.3 from 77.4 Perhaps not unexpectedly, the US vehicle sales dropped back to an annualized rate of 11.2m vehicles in April after the incentive-induced 11.8m units in March. Residential housing is entering a more buoyant period. After spending much of last year and Q1 mired between 500-600,000 units, April data of 672,000 units on an annualized basis was the second successive sharply higher month. While expenditure on residential construction remains around 50% of its peak, the trend is now at least upwards, which requires re-stocking of products throughout the supply chain. ###### **Impact of financial woes on growth yet to be confirmed** ###### **with the eurozone** March Eurozone IP (admittedly a lagging indicator, the April data will be released on June 14) was up 1.3% month-onmonth and was up 6.9% year-on-year – a much stronger performance than expected. This may set the groundwork for further gains with inventory adjustment, a weak euro (and rising exports) and the improvement in global activity acting as supporting factors. On the downside, high (and rising) unemployment as well as budget deficits and the sovereign debt problems may constrain further gains. GFMS notes that business and consumer confidence in the Eurozone fell in May to 98.4 from 100.6 in April. ###### **Slower growth in China, but no collapse** Chinese industrial production grew 17.8% year-on-year in April – down slightly from March’s growth level. Chinese fixed asset investment also continues to slow. Growth fell to 26.1% year-to-April from 26.4% in the first quarter. The decline in credit creation appears to be filtering through, but this level will be exactly what the government is looking for – a soft rather than hard landing. However, Chinese vehicle output continues to surge. Volumes were up 34.6% year-onyear in April after March’s 51.1% gains. OECD Leading Indicators & GFMS Base Metals Index

Independent - Informed - International **C1** Copper - June 2010 ###### **Market background** The few weeks since the release of our previous monthly copper report have seen the European sovereign debt crisis continue to weigh on copper prices. On 19th May, the official spot settlement price on the LME fell to $6,466/tonne, a level unseen since February, although this was still some way from the low registered early in that month. The $6,500/tonne barrier proved to be a strong support level and prices have since then recovered somewhat, even though sentiment towards sovereign debt has not materially improved. By end-month, the $7,000/tonne level had been tested and, on an intra-day basis, exceeded at the margin, but this proved short-lived and prices in early June stand below$6,700/ tonne. the country rose, as direct feed of scrap into fabrication fell considerably. Partly offsetting the 17% increase in local production, net imports of refined copper fell by 4% year-on-year, although at nearly 305,000 tonnes these still stood above long-term norms, both in absolute terms but also when measured as a percentage of local consumption. Overall, apparent consumption (excluding changes in stocks) rose by 7% yearon-year in April and by a combined 8% year-on-year over the January to April period. Against this, semis production growth over the respective period was a much faster 19% and 23%. ###### **...but the market likely remains in surplus** Looking at LME i

nventories, these continued to trend downwards in May. Overall, inventories fell by 21,400 tonnes, to end the month at 475,575 tonnes. Declines were also noted in Shanghai Futures Exchange (SHFE) stocks, which fell by nearly 32,000 tonnes to their end-May level of less than 158,000 tonnes. In spite of the above-mentioned declines in visible copper inventories, GFMS are convinced that the global market remains in surplus. As we note later in this section, in our view, what has likely continued to take place in recent months has been a flow of material from reported to unreported stockpiles, the latter overwhelmingly located in China. ###### **Chinese supply continues to boom...** The latest official data from the CNIA suggests that refined copper production in the country rose by 17% in April to 387,800 tonnes. The increase was fuelled by a 28% rise in local production as well as concentrate imports being up by 17% year-on-year. Although scrap imports (and by implication availability) were down somewhat year-onyear, reports by Antaike, the Chinese government-linked research consultancy, suggest that secondary production in At first look the comparison alludes to sizeable de-stocking having taken place in the country. Nevertheless, it is worth noting the comparison for apparent consumption is made against last year’s exceptionally high base, which was distorted by purchases by the State Reserve Bureau (SRB) as well as private unreported stockpiling of copper. Contrasting these figures, anecdotal information suggests that the Chinese market was in surplus in April. After comparing the gap between semis production and apparent consumption with the net imports of scrap into China, making certain assumptions on copper content, use in secondary production and local scrap generation, GFMS continue to agree with this view. We would stress, nevertheless, that the size of the net oversupply in the market during April and also over the first quarter is bound to be far lower than the one seen over the same period last year. Given the rise in SHFE inventories over the four months in question, we would surmise that much of the excess metal found its way into warehouses registered with the Chinese exchange. More recently, a decline in SHFE stocks as well as ongoing net absorption of metal by China suggests additions may have been made to unreported stockpiles in the country. ###### **Chinese resource tax overhaul to hit local producers** 

Official sources suggest that the Chinese government is currently undertaking an overhaul of its resource tax regime, away from the current fixed amount per volume system to one which is linked to the underlying commodity prices. The tax reform is expected to affect all minerals, including oil, coal, iron ore and nonferrous metals.  Recent reports suggest that the new regime will be implemented in Xinjian region from 1st June and will subsequently spread to the rest of the country.  Naturally, the new tax will increase operating costs of local producers, which until recently had to pay no more than few yuan per tonne of production. Although this may eventually impact on copper prices, the still sizeable gap between current price levels and marginal costs of production suggest that any related increase would be limited. 

###### **ICSG and WBMS data overstate the weakness of mature economies’ consumption** 

The latest statistics by both the ICSG and WBMS continue to illustrate a lack of momentum in the global copper consumption recovery.  The former organisation’s latest monthly bulletin suggests that global demand was up by 5.9% in January and February combined, whereas the latter group’s first quarter estimates show a 5.2% growth in the global figure. 

Looking at the country-by-country breakdown of these figures, GFMS were once again surprised to see demand growth for a number of key mature markets still in negative territory, despite an exceptionally low base last year and our own information confirming noteworthy - in many cases double-digit - growth having taken place in recent months. Noteworthy examples are the United States, where the WBMS data suggests consumption fell by 4.2% year-on-year, Germany, for which the organisation sees demand having 

fallen by 2.3% and France, where demand seems to have collapsed by a further 30% year-on-year.  As we noted in the previous edition of our Base Metals One Year Forecast, we would expect future revisions to these figures to see positive consumption growth for these countries and that this will also result in somewhat stronger growth globally.  It is worth re-iterating here that even after such revisions are in place, we would still expect consumption levels in the first quarter to have been significantly short of historical norms for the majority of mature markets and that this is unlikely to change in the foreseeable future. 

###### **First Quantum loses licence to Frontier and Lonshi mines** 

First Quantum’s legal saga in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) entered a new chapter in late May, as the country’s supreme court annulled the company’s rights to the Frontier and Lonshi mines.  The rights are claimed by state-owned Sociйtй de Dйveloppement Industriel et Minier du Congo (Sodimico).  The former operation, the largest in the country, yielded more than 92,000 tonnes of copper-inconcentrate in 2009.  Mini

ng operations in the latter have been ceased since the open-pit mine was depleted in August 2008, but an underground deposit at the site has been under evaluation. To-date, production at the company’s Frontier mine has continued and it is unclear how the ruling will impact on future output at this stage. ###### **Production growth continues in Chile** Chile’s National Statistics Bureau reported that copper production in the country posted another healthy increase in April. Output was up by 6.4% year-on-year during the month, totalling just under 455,000 tonnes, although refined production fell slightly. Overall, production over the first four months of the year rose by 3.2%, amounting to 1.72 million tonnes. LME Stocks vs Spot Price

Independent - Informed - International **C3** Copper - June 2010 ###### **Market outlook** GFMS have revised the supply and demand estimates for last year as well as our projections and we have extended the latter to the first half of next year. Starting with our 2009 figures, we have revised both our global consumption and production estimates downwards and this has resulted in our surplus estimate having increased to 846,000 tonnes, compared to the 777,000 tonne figure featured in our Copper Survey as well as our previous Monthly report. Independent - Informed - International **N1** Nickel & Cobalt - June 2010 ###### **Market background** At the time of our last Base Metals One Year Forecast, prices were undergoing a correction, which came following nickel’s somewhat inflated rise to $27,600/tonne in mid April. Notably, since the peak, the spot price has fallen by around 30% to below $19,500/tonne on June 3. Debt problems surrounding various European economies combined with bearish currency sentiment, more specifically a pressurised euro, have seen investors pull out of risky assets. This has indeed added to the downward momentum. Market fundamentals suggest some support once the “across the board” selling pressure has ended. On the demandside, global stainless steel production is trending higher. Although, destocking associated with lower surcharges may curb output growth in the summer months. On the supplyside, apart from growth in Chinese nickel pig iron production, output remains largely muted. The strike at Vale’s Canadian operations also continues to persist. Furthermore, LME inventories have continued to trend lower since the last time we reported them. At below 138,000 tonnes in early June, they are down by over 28,000 tonnes since reaching an all-time high of 166,476 tonnes on February 5. ###### **ISSF data confirms robust stainless production growth over the first quarter** As we highlighted in our last Base Metals One Year Forecast, a number of stainless steel markets had been recovering from the global downturn. In particular, the mature economies had seen vast improvements over the first quarter. The latest data by the International Stainless Steel Forum (ISSF) indeed confirms this. According to the organisation, 7.472 million tonnes of stainless steel were produced globally over the first quarter of 2010, almost the highest ever volume for the first three months of a year. Moreover, this represented growth of 54.6% year-on-year. Notably, every region experienced growth in excess of +37%, but the Americas was the star performer registering growth of some 79.1% year-on-year. Asia (excluding China) and Western Europe/Africa followed with growth of 68.0% and 57.4%, respectively, while both China and Central and Eastern Europe produced around 37% more than in the same period last year. While impressive, the year-on-year comparisons reflect a number of factors. First and most importantly, production in the first quarter of 2009 was hit by the global downturn. This, as a result, saw output fall almost to the lowest level in a decade. Therefore,

the 2010 first quarter growth figure seems exceptionally high. Second, after very strong destocking last year, improved market conditions have encouraged consumers to replenish their stocks. Rising end-use demand, however, also contributed to the rise in the first quarter. Looking ahead, the ISSF estimates that global stainless steel production will increase by around 11-12% this year. This is roughly in line with our own projections, which in turn, underpin GFMS’ nickel consumption forecast close to 9% demand growth this year. Recent data from ThyssenKrupp (TKS) and Arcelor Mittal (AM) highlight the steps taken by individual producers to lift output. TKS stated that its utilisation rate is now in the range of 80-90%. Actual output in the first quarter was 9%, up on the final three months of last year at 657,000 tonnes. AM raised its output by 21% to 546,000 tonnes. Reflecting the exceptionally low level of production a year earlier, output was up by 109% and 72%, respectively. China’s crude stainless output grew by 9% quarter-onquarter and 38% year-on-year to 2.44 million tonnes, according to the Stainless Steel Council of China. It should be noted however from a nickel demand perspective that the growth for austenitic grades, quarter-on-quarter growth was minimal at just 0.2%, compared to expansion of 25% and 10% for 400 and 200 series, respectively. Imports were affected as domestic market supply started rising in March as Ta

igang finished a major government order. In terms of prices, after plunging in the week ending May 21, Chinese spot prices for stainless steel sheet in the Foshan market have regained some ground. Also, anecdotal evidence suggests that despite the correction in stainless steel prices, demand remains weak. Baosteel has suggested that curbs on the Chinese property sector, a strengthening of the exchange rate and lower export demand have seen underlying demand growth slow. ###### **Strong stainless steel production filters through to high global nickel demand in Q1** In line with a sharp recovery in stainless steel production, global nickel demand has increased markedly over the first three months of the year. b, down 12.8% from the recent high of $23.50/lb. However, low-grade prices have fallen much sharply as euro zone problems loom larger. In terms of terminal market stocks, inventories on the LME have increased to 115 tonnes on June 3. ###### **Production will continue trending higher…** As noted in our last Base Metals One Year Forecast, the supply side of the market will continue seeing higher production as producers boost output especially in the African copper-cobalt belt. The company, which has a 57.75% share in Tenke Fungurume, is Congo’s largest private investment. It is estimated that the mine produced 29,000 tonnes of copper and 2,300 tonnes of cobalt over the first quarter of 2010, on track to break a year-end target of 115,000 tonnes of copper and 8,000 tonnes of cobalt. We have reduced our estimates of the deficit for the first and second quarters of this year. We have the cobalt market in modest surplus in the second half, partly on the assumption of higher output at Vale’s operations and in the African copper-cobalt belt. Although the decline in cobalt has not been as significant as for some of the other LME-traded metals, prices have fallen by around 15% from recent highs. Given a still reasonably tight supply-demand balance position, we are only projecting a relatively small decline in prices from those prevailing in early June of around $20-21/lb.
